1.1:
Rahmah El Yunusiyyah was born in 1900 in Bukit Surungan, Padang Panjang, West Sumatra, then part of the Dutch East Indies. Her birthday is given differently: 26 October 1900 (Wikipedia's article on her) or 20 or 29 December 1900 (Indonesian sources), so the game gives only the year.

The notes in this game come from the histories cited in Wikipedia's article "Rahmah el Yunusiyah" (Audrey Kahin, Jeffrey Hadler's Muslims and Matriarchs, Pieternella van Doorn-Harder's Women Shaping Islam, and others) and from Fitriyanti et al., Journal of Educational Sciences 10(1), 2026.
1.2: She was the youngest child of a Minangkabau family of Islamic scholars. Her father, Muhammad Yunus, was a qadi (judge); her mother was Rafi'ah. Her grandfather was a well-known scholar and astronomer.
1.3: The Minangkabau are matrilineal: family and property pass through the mother's line. The 2026 article points out the paradox Rahmah saw: women were honoured in Minangkabau custom, yet had little access to religious education.
2.2: After her father died, his former students taught her. She learned to read and write in Arabic script and in Latin script (most likely Arabic and Malay in Jawi, and Malay in Latin letters).
2.4: She had some training in midwifery at a local hospital.
3.1: Her family arranged for her to be married in 1916, at about sixteen, to a scholar, Bahauddin Lathif, and she had to leave school. In 1922 her husband married two more wives; she obtained a divorce and went back to her education. They had no children. The game says only that she had to leave school.
3.2: From 1918 she studied Islam in private study circles.
4.1: Her brother Zainuddin Labay el Yunusi had founded the Diniyah School, for boys and girls, in 1915.
4.2: Her study circle for the girls was influenced by Ruhana Kuddus's women's association, Amai Setia, and was called the Women and Girls' Association.
4.4: She was unhappy with the Islamic education girls could get, and with the ways mixed schools kept them from taking full part.
5.1: Diniyah Putri (also called Madrasah Diniyah li al-Banat) opened on 1 November 1923. It is generally thought to be the first Islamic school for girls in the Indies; the 2026 article calls it the first Islamic educational institution exclusively for women in Southeast Asia.
5.3: The first 71 students were mostly young housewives. The lessons were basic Islamic education, Arabic grammar, some modern subjects and handicrafts; later also health, sewing, leadership, English, history and geography.
6.1: She faced hostility and criticism: not everyone accepted a modern school for girls.
6.2: She consulted the local scholars before opening the school, and believed that Islam demanded a central role for women and for women's education.
6.3: Her brother Zainuddin, who had supported the school, died in 1924.
7.1: The Padang Panjang earthquakes of 1926 destroyed the school building. The game leaves out the people who died in them.
7.3: Muhammadiyah, a large Islamic organisation, offered to take over the school and rebuild it; she said no, and toured the Indies to raise the money herself. The new building opened in 1928.
8.1: She would not accept Dutch government subsidies, so that the school's dress, calendar and lessons could stay centred on Islam. Like the Taman Siswa schools, she had to fight the Dutch rules against "wild" (unlicensed) schools, and she was fined for discussing politics.
8.2: By the end of the 1930s the school had about 500 students. The historian Audrey Kahin calls Diniyah Putri "one of the most successful and influential of the schools for women" before independence.
8.3: Kulliyatul Muallimat al-Islamiyyah, a college for women teachers, opened in 1937. She also founded schools in Jakarta (1935) and a high school in Padang Panjang (1938).
9.1: Indonesia's independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945. During the Japanese occupation before it, she led a local defence unit (Giyugun) in Padang Panjang, and campaigned against the Japanese use of Indonesian women as "comfort women".
9.2:
During the war of independence that followed, she set up supplies for the Republic's side. The Dutch held her prisoner for seven months in 1949.

In 1955 she was elected to parliament for the Masyumi party, one of the first women in it. She later supported the PRRI, a rebellion against the central government (1958), lost her seat, and was arrested in 1961, then freed under an amnesty. The game leaves her politics out.
10.1: The Grand Imam of al-Azhar, Abd al-Rahman Taj, visited the school: in 1956 according to Wikipedia, 1955 according to other sources.
10.4: Syaikhah is the feminine of shaykh: a title for a great scholar. Wikipedia gives 1957, after her Hajj; the 2026 article gives 1955. Both say no woman had been given it before. The game gives no year.
10.5: After her visit, Egypt gave scholarships for Diniyah Putri graduates to study at al-Azhar.
11.1: The women's Islamic university was opened in 1967 by the governor of West Sumatra, Harun Zain.
11.2: She died on 26 February 1969. Her grave, in the grounds of the school's boarding house, is a protected heritage site.
11.4: President Prabowo Subianto named her a National Hero of Indonesia in November 2025. The award was received by Fauziah Fauzan El Muhammady, head of the Diniyyah Puteri school today.
